title: Rethinking how we Scaffold AI Agents - Rahul Sengottuvelu, Ramp

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The speaker explicitly states the ideas generalize: backends are all request-response, the three-approach framework applies broadly, and the LLM-as-backend model is proposed as a general software architecture pattern.

domains.label: Finance & Trading
domains.rationale: Ramp is a finance platform for expense management, payments, procurement, and travel. The featured production system (switching report) ingests card-provider transaction CSVs for onboarding, a finance-domain use case.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: Ramp automates back-office work for finance teams and employees: expense reports, reimbursements, flight/hotel booking. The switching report helps migrate enterprise financial data from legacy systems.

summary: Rahul Sengottuvelu (Head of Applied AI at Ramp) advances one thesis: AI agents should be scaffolded so they scale with compute, not with hand-crafted code, because 'systems that scale with compute beat systems that don't.' He frames this as the Bitter Lesson and notes exponentials are rare-when you find one, 'hitch the ride.' He cites chess, go, computer vision, and Atari, where hand-built features win only at fixed compute but general methods win once search scales. The concrete example is Ramp's 'switching report' agent, which ingests arbitrary CSVs from third-party card providers and maps them into Ramp's transaction schema. He contrasts three architectures: (1) manually coding parsers for the 50 most common vendors (rigid, breaks on format changes, with an over-engineered ~100,000-line variant); (2) classical scripting augmented with light LLM/embedding calls to classify each CSV column (date, amount, merchant, user) and map it; and (3) giving the CSV to an LLM with a code interpreter, a target format, and a unit-test verifier. The third fails if run once but 'works really well' run fifty times in parallel, generalizing across formats despite roughly 10,000x more compute-still under a dollar, far cheaper than engineer time or a failed migration. He abstracts this as black arrows (classical compute) versus blue arrows (neural/'fuzzy'/latent-space compute). Approach 3 flips control: the LLM decides when to drop into classical land (writing pandas/Python), and most compute is blue. Because big labs keep improving models, blue-arrow code improves for free, so maximizing it lets your system benefit with no engineering effort. Backends are fundamentally request-response, making this generalizable. He pushes the idea to an 'LLM-as-backend' model where the LM itself executes, with code-interpreter, network, and database tools. A live demo renders a Gmail-like email client from markdown, handles clicks by telling the LM what was selected, and lets it render like a web framework. He concedes it 'barely works today' (a delete failed live) but speculates exponential trends may make such software 'take off,' ending uncertain whether more software will look like this.
whyItMatters: The talk weaves together a strategic principle (the Bitter Lesson / compute scaling), a concrete production system (the switching report CSV-mapping agent), and a forward-looking architecture (LLM-as-backend). The software-engineering concepts explain HOW the three architectures differ-control flow, verifier placement, and where classical vs neural compute lives-while the AI concepts explain WHY one should prefer the compute-scaling architecture: parallel sampling plus a self-checking verifier turns an unreliable one-shot LLM into a generalizing agent whose performance keeps improving for free as models advance. The control-flow inversion (the LLM decides when to write classical code) is the hinge that connects the CSV case study to the LLM-as-backend proposal, and the request-response generalization is what lets the speaker claim the pattern applies broadly. Taken together, the concepts form a single argument: architect agents so that as much computation as possible is neural and scales with compute, because that share improves without engineering effort.
temporalContext: The talk was recorded at AI Engineer Summit 2025 (Agent Engineering Session Day, Feb 21, 2025, NYC) and the video was published 2025-03-19. As of the research_as_of date (2026-08-16), the speaker's role has evolved from Head of Applied AI to CTO of Ramp (promotion announced 2026-06-25), and Ramp Labs has published analogous parallel-LLM-agent research (Agent Fill) that corroborates the approach-3 architecture described in the talk. No factual claims in the transcript have been contradicted by later evidence; the LLM-as-backend demo's 'barely works today' caveat remains accurate as of the research date.
takeaways: The talk's single core idea: systems that scale with compute beat systems that don't-an application of Sutton's Bitter Lesson to agent scaffolding.
Exponentials are rare; when you find one, 'hitch the ride' rather than over-engineer clever features against it.
History (chess, go, Atari, computer vision) shows hand-crafted features win only at fixed compute; general methods that scale search always win once compute scales.
Ramp's 'switching report' illustrates three architectures: hand-code per vendor; classical + light LLM column classification; and an LLM with a code interpreter run 50x in parallel.
The code-interpreter approach fails if run once but generalizes well run 50x in parallel, despite ~10,000x more compute-still under $1, far cheaper than engineer time or a failed migration.
'Blue arrows' (neural/fuzzy compute) improve for free as labs keep training better models; maximizing blue-arrow share lets a system improve with no engineering effort.
Backends are fundamentally request-response; the third architecture flips control so the LLM decides when to drop into classical compute (writing pandas/Python).
Proposed 'LLM-as-backend': the LM itself is the execution backend, with tools (code interpreter), network access, and database access.
Live demo: an LLM-driven email client renders Gmail-like UI from markdown and handles clicks by telling the LM what was clicked, letting it render like a web framework.
The LLM-as-backend software 'barely works today' and a live action failed, but exponential trends may make such architectures take off-the speaker is uncertain it will catch on.

concepts.name: The Bitter Lesson (Sutton)
concepts.explanation: Rich Sutton's thesis that general methods leveraging computation ultimately outperform methods encoding human knowledge, because compute scales. The speaker adopts this as the talk's central idea and applies it to agent scaffolding.
concepts.importance: Provides the theoretical frame for the entire talk; the switching report case study is presented as evidence for the Bitter Lesson applied to agents.

concepts.name: Compute Scaling
concepts.explanation: The principle that systems whose performance scales with available compute will over time beat systems that do not, even if the latter are cleverer at fixed compute. The speaker treats exponentials as rare and worth exploiting.
concepts.importance: The core criterion the speaker uses to judge agent architectures: does the architecture scale with compute?

concepts.name: Constrained Decoding (Jsonformer)
concepts.explanation: Techniques that force an LLM to produce output conforming to a schema (e.g., valid JSON). The speaker authored Jsonformer, an early scaffolding library built because models were too unreliable at structured output; an example of scaffolding that gets deleted as models improve.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the historical pattern of building scaffolding around weak models and removing it as they improve, motivating compute-scaling architectures.

concepts.name: Code Interpreter Agents
concepts.explanation: Agents that are given a code interpreter so they can write and execute code (pandas, Python, Rust-based libraries) to solve a task rather than emitting a direct answer. Approach 3 gives the LLM the CSV and a code interpreter to transform it.
concepts.importance: The mechanism that turns an unreliable one-shot LLM into a reliable, generalizing agent when combined with parallel sampling and a verifier.

concepts.name: Parallel Sampling (Run-50x)
concepts.explanation: Running the same agent many times in parallel and selecting a passing result. The code-interpreter approach fails if run once but generalizes well across formats when run ~50 times in parallel.
concepts.importance: The brute-compute remedy that makes approach 3 reliable; the key technique the speaker advocates and the basis for the cost analysis.

concepts.name: LLM-as-Backend
concepts.explanation: A proposed architecture where the LM itself is the execution backend: it receives requests and uses tools (code interpreter, network, database) to produce responses and render UI, rather than a hand-coded backend calling the model.
concepts.importance: The talk's forward-looking proposal and the demo subject; the ultimate expression of maximizing neural compute share.

concepts.name: Latent-Space / Fuzzy Compute (Blue Arrows)
concepts.explanation: The speaker's abstraction of neural, 'fuzzy,' latent-space computation (blue arrows) versus deterministic classical computation (black arrows). Maximizing blue-arrow share means more of the system improves for free as labs train better models.
concepts.importance: The mental model the speaker uses to reason about which parts of a system will improve without engineering effort.

concepts.name: Embedding Similarity / Column Classification
concepts.explanation: Approach 2 augments classical scripting with LLM/embedding calls to classify each CSV column (date, amount, merchant, user) by semantic similarity and then map it. A middle-ground architecture that adds some neural compute to a classical backbone.
concepts.importance: Represents the industry-typical middle architecture the speaker contrasts with the compute-scaling approach 3.

concepts.name: Exponential Trends / Free-Ride on Model Improvement
concepts.explanation: The argument that because big labs spend billions improving models, the neural-compute share of your system improves for free with no engineering effort-so you should 'hitch the ride' on exponential trends rather than over-engineer against them.
concepts.importance: The strategic justification for maximizing blue-arrow compute; ties the engineering choice to the economics of frontier-model improvement.

concepts.name: Agent Scaffolding
concepts.explanation: The code wrapped around an LLM to make it work reliably (prompt construction, tool wiring, control flow, validation). The speaker's central architectural concern is building agent scaffolding that scales with model intelligence rather than hand-coded logic that must be deleted as models improve.
concepts.importance: Frames the entire talk: scaffolding that scales with compute (and gets deleted as models improve) is preferred over rigid scaffolding that fights the model.

concepts.name: Request-Response Backend
concepts.explanation: The observation that backends are fundamentally request-response: a message goes in, the backend transforms it, and a response comes back. The speaker uses this to argue the LLM-as-backend pattern is generalizable across systems.
concepts.importance: Provides the generalization bridge from the CSV-parsing agent to the LLM-as-backend proposal, arguing the architecture applies broadly.

concepts.name: CSV Schema Mapping (Switching Report)
concepts.explanation: The data-integration problem of taking arbitrary-format CSVs from third-party card providers and mapping their columns into Ramp's canonical transaction schema. The switching report is the anchoring production use case for comparing three architectures.
concepts.importance: Concrete production problem that grounds the abstract architectural thesis in a measurable reliability/cost tradeoff.

concepts.name: Per-Vendor Hand-Coded Parsers
concepts.explanation: Approach 1: manually writing a separate parser for each of the 50 most common third-party card vendors. Brittle because any vendor format change breaks the parser and pages an engineer; an over-engineered variant reached ~100,000 lines of code.
concepts.importance: Represents the rigid, hand-crafted baseline the Bitter-Lesson argument is set against; illustrates the maintenance cost of non-scaling code.

concepts.name: Unit-Test Verifier / Self-Checking
concepts.explanation: In approach 3 the agent is given a target output format plus a unit test / verifier it can run to tell whether its transformation is correct before returning. This lets the agent self-check candidate solutions.
concepts.importance: The verifier is the mechanism that makes parallel sampling viable: each of the 50 runs can be checked, and a passing one selected.

concepts.name: Control-Flow Inversion (LLM-Driven Classical Compute)
concepts.explanation: In approach 3 the control plane is inverted: instead of classical code calling the LLM in narrow spots, the LLM decides when to drop into classical compute by writing and executing pandas/Python itself. Most compute becomes 'fuzzy' (neural), with classical compute invoked on demand.
concepts.importance: The architectural insight that maximizes the share of compute that improves for free as models advance, and that distinguishes approach 3 from approaches 1 and 2.

sections.summary: Speaker introduces himself, four years on LLMs, early customer-support chatbot with GPT-2/BERT, writing then deleting scaffolding code, and Jsonformer.

sections.title: Core idea: the Bitter Lesson & historical examples
sections.summary: States the one idea-systems that scale with compute win; exponentials are rare so hitch the ride; chess/go/Atari/CV show general methods beat hand-crafted features at scale.

sections.title: Ramp overview
sections.summary: Describes Ramp as a finance platform automating expenses, payments, procurement, travel, bookkeeping with heavy AI and legacy-system integration.

sections.title: Switching report: three architectures
sections.summary: Introduces the switching report (parse arbitrary CSVs to Ramp schema) and contrasts hand-coded, classical-plus-LLM, and code-interpreter-run-50x approaches with cost analysis.

sections.title: Generalizing the three approaches
sections.summary: Maps the approaches onto black (classical) vs blue (fuzzy) arrows; argues approach 3 flips control to the LLM and blue arrows improve for free as labs advance models.

sections.title: LLM-as-backend proposal
sections.summary: Contrasts a traditional web app with a model where the backend IS the LM, with code-interpreter, network, and DB tools.

sections.title: Email client live demo
sections.summary: Live demo of an LLM-driven Gmail-like client rendering markdown UI, handling clicks as LM prompts; concedes it barely works today but may take off on exponential trends.

demonstrations: Ramp 'switching report' CSV-parsing agent (three architectures): A production Ramp agent that ingests arbitrary-format CSVs from third-party card providers and maps them into Ramp's transaction schema. Three architectures compared: hand-coded per-vendor parsers for 50 vendors; classical scripting plus LLM/embedding column classification; and an LLM with a code interpreter, target format, and unit-test verifier run 50x in parallel.

LLM-as-backend email client (live demo): A custom email client where the Gmail token is sent to an LLM that simulates a Gmail client, rendering a homepage UI as markdown from live audience emails. Clicking an email tells the LM the clicked text and ID; the LM renders the page like a web framework. A delete action failed live; the speaker said this software 'barely works today.'
limitations: Approach 3 (code-interpreter agent) does not work if run only once; it requires ~50 parallel runs to reliably succeed.
The LLM-as-backend email client barely works today and was slow; a delete action failed during the live demo.
The speaker explicitly expresses uncertainty about adoption: Will more software look like this? I don't know, we'll see.
The engineer-time-is-scarce argument is explicitly time-bound by the speaker (maybe not for a while but at least today).
The speaker caveats his own blue/black-arrow visualization as maybe not the most accurate graph.
Historical-game analogies (chess, go, Atari, CV) are asserted, not proven, as evidence for the agent-architecture thesis.
quantitativeClaims: Speaker has worked on LLMs for about four years.
Approach 1 manually codes parsers for the 50 most common third-party card vendors.
Over-engineered hand-coded variant reached about 100,000 lines of code.
Approach 3 runs the code-interpreter agent 50 times in parallel.
Approach 3 uses roughly 10,000 times more compute than approach 1.
The extra compute for approach 3 costs less than a dollar per run.
Big labs are spending billions improving models, so blue-arrow compute improves for free.
OpenAI makes billions of dollars (scale of fuzzy-compute usage in industry).

organization.name: Ramp
organization.summary: Ramp is an independent private finance-operations company (no parent), founded 2019, HQ New York. It provides spend management, corporate cards, expense management, payments, procurement, travel, and bookkeeping automation. Ramp builds its own AI agents across the product to automate finance-team and employee workflows. The talk's featured production system (the switching report CSV-parsing agent) is owned by Ramp's Applied AI team, which the speaker led at video time (Head of Applied AI) and now leads as CTO (2026).
organization.status: Active and independent; speaker promoted from Head of Applied AI to CTO in June 2026.

technologies.label: Code-Interpreter Agent with Parallel Sampling
technologies.summary: Approach 3 in the talk: give the raw input (e.g., a CSV) to an LLM that has a code interpreter, a target output format, and a unit-test verifier. The LLM writes and executes pandas/Python to transform the input, and the system runs the agent many times in parallel (run-50x), selecting a result that passes the verifier. This fails as a single shot but generalizes across arbitrary formats when parallelized, at roughly 10,000x the compute of hand-coding yet under a dollar per run-far cheaper than engineer time or a failed migration.
technologies.role: The architecture the speaker advocates (approach 3), demonstrated via Ramp's switching report production agent.

technologies.label: LLM-as-Backend
technologies.summary: A proposed architecture where the LM itself is the execution backend. Instead of a hand-coded backend that calls the model in narrow spots, the LM receives requests, has tool access (code interpreter, network, database), and produces responses and renders UI directly. The email-client demo renders a Gmail-like UI from markdown and handles clicks by telling the LM what was selected, letting it render like a web framework.
technologies.role: The talk's forward-looking proposal, demonstrated live with an email client that barely works today.

technologies.label: Constrained Decoding (Jsonformer)
technologies.summary: Techniques that force an LLM to produce output conforming to a schema (e.g., valid JSON). The speaker authored Jsonformer, an early constrained-decoding library built because models were too unreliable at structured output-an example of scaffolding built around weak models that the Bitter-Lesson argument predicts will be removed as models improve.
technologies.role: Background context for the speaker's scaffolding philosophy; an early library he built and later removed as models improved.

prerequisites: Familiarity with LLMs, prompting, and the concept of an AI agent.
Basic understanding of web backends, request-response, and CRUD operations.
Awareness of Sutton's Bitter Lesson is helpful (the talk summarizes it).
Comfort with Python/pandas and the idea of a code interpreter.
General familiarity with embeddings/semantic similarity and constrained/structured output.
outcomes: Articulate why compute-scaling systems outperform rigid, hand-coded ones, using the Bitter Lesson as framing.
Compare three agent architectures (hand-coded, classical-plus-LLM, code-interpreter-with-parallel-sampling) and their compute/effort tradeoffs.
Justify parallel sampling (run-50x) as a brute-compute remedy for unreliable single-shot LLM tasks, and reason about its cost (~<$1) versus engineer time.
Reason about the blue-arrow vs black-arrow compute mix and why maximizing neural compute lets a system improve for free as models advance.
Describe the LLM-as-backend pattern, its tool access (code interpreter, network, DB), and its current reliability limitations as shown in the email demo.
Evaluate when hand-crafted heuristics are justified (fixed compute wins) versus when compute-scaling approaches dominate (search scales).
Critically assess the speaker's thesis, including the latency caveat and the uncertainty about whether LLM-as-backend will catch on.
challengeSeeds: Design an agent that scales with compute: architect a system where the neural/fuzzy compute share is maximized and classical hand-coding is minimized, with justification for each boundary.
The 100-vendor long tail: extend the switching report beyond the top 50 card vendors to truly arbitrary CSV schemas, testing generalization without per-vendor code.
Latency-budget challenge: constrain the switching report to a 5-second response time while maintaining reliability, forcing a tradeoff between parallel sampling (run 50x) and latency.
Critical-response debate: steelman the counter-position that hand-crafted heuristics are preferable when compute is fixed or when latency matters.
